expectations.text: States plainly that the not-empty check is insufficient
expectations.evidence: "No — that test wouldn't have caught this bug. The table wasn't empty; it was full of coalesced zeros."

expectations.text: Identifies the COALESCE to zero as the mechanism that made the failure silent
expectations.evidence: "**Silent coercion** — `COALESCE(x, 0)` masked nulls as plausible values"

expectations.text: Recommends reconciliation against a source of truth, not only shape checks
expectations.evidence: "Reconciliation: compare sum to upstream source of truth | Yes — catches drift"

expectations.text: Recommends that assertions run before publication rather than after, so bad data cannot reach the dashboard
expectations.evidence: Says "Add to your pipeline tests" and "assert expected columns exist before join" (ordering within the job), but never states that assertions must gate publication/blocking bad data from reaching the dashboard — no mention of failing the run before publishing, staging/swap, or circuit-breaking the load.

expectations.text: Recommends a data contract or schema check so an upstream rename fails loudly and attributably
expectations.evidence: "Schema contract test: assert expected columns exist before join | Yes — fails fast on rename" and "The schema contract is the real fix"

expectations.text: Recommends volume or null-rate assertions rather than only a non-empty check
expectations.evidence: "Null rate assertion: revenue column null% < 1%" and "Row count bounds: expect 10k–50k rows, not just >0"

expectations.text: Treats three weeks of nobody noticing as a detection gap worth its own fix
expectations.evidence: "**No anomaly detection** — 3 weeks of 'low but okay' didn't trigger anything" — listed as its own failure with detection controls (statistical bound, reconciliation) proposed

expectations.text: Explains why a silently wrong number is more dangerous than a failed pipeline
expectations.evidence: Notes zeros looked "plausible" and that "'Not empty' catches complete outages, not partial data corruption," but never explains why silent wrongness is more dangerous than an outright failure — no reasoning about a loud failure being safer/self-announcing versus wrong numbers being trusted and acted on.
